The Dog cockle Glycymeris glycymeris, a common bivalve inhabiting sandy sublittoral substrates, exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a relatively slow-growing, long-lived marine mollusc. In populations from the northeastern Atlantic, individuals typically attain a maximum shell height of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], a measurement that represents the ultimate vertical dimension of the adult valve. Field surveys indicate that sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is initiated when the shell reaches a length of approximately 3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3 centimeters]. This size at puberty suggests that individuals invest considerable somatic growth before allocating resources towards reproductive tissues. The growth trajectory leading to the maximum recorded valve height is gradual, with annual increments in shell length decreasing markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, a common pattern observed among iteroparous bivalves with determinate growth phases. The ultimate shell height of this species places it among the larger members of the Glycymerididae family within its geographical range.

Regarding the earliest life stages, the initial wet weight at birth, corresponding to the moment of hatching from an egg characterized by a diameter of roughly 55 micrometers, is remarkably low at 0.000000058 grams [Wwb = 0.000000058 grams]. This minute mass reflects the lecithotrophic nature of the early veliger larva, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for its initial development. The newly hatched larva, a free-swimming planktotrophic veliger, begins exogenous feeding upon phytoplankton shortly after the absorption of its yolk supply. The size at metamorphosis, a critical transition when the planktonic larva settles and undergoes a profound morphological transformation to a benthic juvenile, occurs at a shell length of 0.1 centimeters . This larval-juvenile transition marks the end of the planktonic phase and the beginning of infaunal life, a major ecological shift during which the animal secretes a prodissoconch and commences filter-feeding within the sediment.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of its typical habitat, where the mean annual water temperature hovers around 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the species is characterized by an exceptionally extended lifespan. Analyses of shell growth rings and mark-recapture studies have consistently shown that the oldest documented individuals can survive for approximately 75 years [am = approximately 75 years], a longevity that ranks among the highest recorded for bivalves of c at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]omparable size. This remarkable maximum lifespan is achieved through a combination of low metabolic rates, efficient energy use, and a robust shell that resists predation and physical abrasion. The longevity of Glycymeris glycymeris stands in strong contrast to many co-occurring bivalves, such as members of the Mytilidae, which rarely exceed a decade of life. Such a life span necessitates a high degree of physiological resilience to endure the vicissitudes of the benthic environment. The extended lifespan is also reflected in a prolonged reproductive window, with mature individuals contributing to successive spawning seasons over many decades, thereby ensuring that a steady supply of gametes is released into the water column each year.

Reproductive output in Glycymeris glycymeris is highly seasonal, with spawning events concentrated during the warmer months. The maximum reproductive rate, a calculation of the number of eggs released per spawning, peaks at roughly 500,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 500,000 eggs per spawning event] with approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year] when the ambient water temperature is 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This daily fecundity, combined with a protracted spawning period, results in a substantial lifetime egg production that compensates for the high mortality rates experienced by planktonic larvae during the sensitive dispersal phase. The reproductive strategy of the Dog cockle is thus one of high fecundity and broadcast spawning, a common approach among bivalves that offsets the stochastic survival of offspring in a variable pelagic environment. The synchronization of this spawning effort with periods of optimal phytoplankton abundance likely increases larval feeding success and subsequent recruitment into the juvenile population. The substantial number of eggs released per event ensures that despite high larval mortality, enough individuals survive to maintain stable populations in areas with suitable substrate and food availability.

Concerning the total mass of a fully grown individual, the ultimate dry weight of a mature adult with a shell height of 6.5 centimeters has been measured at approximately 0.54 grams . This value represents the maximum somatic mass of soft tissues after removal of all water, providing a key metric for estimating the standing biomass of a population. The relationship between shell morphometrics and tissue mass is allometric, generally scaling as a power function of shell dimensions, and this dry weight serves as an important parameter for comparative studies of secondary production. Moreover, the total nitrogen and carbon content locked within this body mass allows for an estimation of the species' functional role in benthic nutrient cycling. In many locations, the Dog cockle forms dense beds of high biomass, exerting a significant top-down control on phytoplankton stocks through its filter-feeding activity, and its ecological footprint is directly tied to the accumulation of this adult body mass. These dense aggregations also provide habitat complexity and shelter for a range of associated infaunal and epifaunal organisms, further highlighting the ecological importance of this long-lived bivalve.
